cls: Lipid-lowering agent - bile acid sequestrant (anion-exchange resin)
pharm: An insoluble anion-exchange resin that binds bile acids in the intestine, preventing their reabsorption and increasing hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids, which lowers LDL cholesterol

summary: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant anion-exchange resin used to lower elevated LDL cholesterol (primary hypercholesterolaemia) and to relieve pruritus associated with partial biliary obstruction/cholestasis. It is not absorbed and works in the gut by binding bile acids to form an insoluble complex excreted in the faeces; this depletes the bile acid pool, upregulates hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids and increases LDL-receptor activity, lowering circulating LDL. It is given as a powder mixed with fluid, usually 4 g once or twice daily titrated up to 8-16 g/day (occasionally up to about 24 g/day). The main adverse effects are gastrointestinal (constipation, bloating). It can bind and reduce absorption of many co-administered drugs and fat-soluble vitamins, so other medicines should be taken at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after cholestyramine.
indications: Adjunct to diet for reduction of elevated serum cholesterol in primary hypercholesterolaemia
Relief of pruritus associated with partial biliary obstruction / cholestasis
Other uses include management of bile acid diarrhoea (per local guidance)

moa: Cholestyramine is a quaternary ammonium anion-exchange resin that releases chloride ions and binds negatively charged bile acids in the intestinal lumen, forming an insoluble, non-absorbable complex that is excreted in the faeces. Removing bile acids interrupts their enterohepatic recirculation and stimulates hepatic 7-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing conversion of cholesterol to bile acids. The resulting fall in hepatic cholesterol upregulates LDL receptors on hepatocytes, enhancing clearance of LDL from the blood and lowering serum LDL cholesterol. In cholestasis, removing accumulated bile acids relieves the associated pruritus.

absolute: Complete biliary obstruction (bile acids not secreted into the gut)
Hypersensitivity to cholestyramine or any component
relative: Constipation or history of bowel obstruction; haemorrhoids
Risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency or bleeding disorders
monitor: Bowel function and signs of obstruction
Fat-soluble vitamin status (A, D, E, K) and INR on long-term/high-dose use

preg: Cholestyramine is not systemically absorbed and is not expected to harm the fetus directly. However, prolonged use may reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and folic acid in the mother, which could affect the pregnancy; vitamin supplementation should be considered if used during pregnancy.
lact: Cholestyramine is not absorbed and is not expected to be present in breast milk. With prolonged maternal use, attention to the mother's fat-soluble vitamin status is advisable as reduced maternal vitamin absorption could theoretically affect milk content.
renal: Cholestyramine is not absorbed systemically, so renal impairment does not require dose adjustment. The resin releases chloride, and high doses can occasionally contribute to hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, which is more relevant in patients with renal compromise.
hepatic: Used to relieve pruritus in partial cholestasis, but it is ineffective and contraindicated in complete biliary obstruction because no bile acids reach the intestine. Monitor for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency in cholestatic patients.

major: Reduces absorption and effect of many drugs - separate dosing by at least 1 h before or 4-6 h after; important examples include warfarin (monitor INR), digoxin, levothyroxine and thyroid hormones
Can bind oral contraceptives, reducing their effectiveness
moderate: Reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and folic acid
Reduces absorption of thiazide diuretics, statins, some NSAIDs, mycophenolate, propranolol and many others
Reduces absorption of leflunomide/teriflunomide (used as an elimination procedure - in that context the effect is intended)
minor: May reduce absorption of iron and other minerals
interactions.food: Mix with fluid and take with meals (for lipid lowering); high-fat malabsorption effects relate to bile acid binding
interactions.diagnostics: May lower fat-soluble vitamin levels and alter INR; can affect lipid measurements (intended therapeutic effect)

emergency: Significant bleeding from vitamin K deficiency

missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember with food and fluid, unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not double the dose. Continue to keep other medicines separated from your cholestyramine doses.
overdose: The most likely consequence of overdose is gastrointestinal obstruction; the risk depends on bowel transit and the amount taken. Management is supportive, with attention to relieving obstruction and correcting any electrolyte/acid-base disturbance; the resin itself is not absorbed.
